metadata.title: The impact of the pandemic and school closures on non-cognitive characteristics: Evidence from PISA
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses pooled PISA microdata across 2012–2022 for non-cognitive outcomes, restricting the non-cognitive measures to those available consistently over time (BELONG from 2012 onward; Growth Mindset and Bullied frequently from 2018 onward). To mitigate cross-national representativeness concerns, the authors state that they implement weights at the student level, and they follow OECD-recommended Balance Repeated Replication (RBB) procedures for inference. The paper does not report the exact weight variable name(s) in the provided text, but it explicitly indicates student-level weighting and clustered standard errors at the school level. Because the analysis is conducted with OLS regressions rather than ML algorithms, the weighting is used for population-representative estimation and standard error computation rather than for model training.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are non-cognitive indices and survey-based constructs (sense of belonging, growth mindset, and a bullying exposure indicator) derived from PISA questionnaire items and IRT-based indices, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. As a result, the paper does not describe plausible-value (PV) handling in the way typical for PISA cognitive domains. The manuscript also does not report a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain item nonresponse; however, the authors’ focus on index construction and regression specifications does not provide enough methodological detail to determine the exact approach.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis pools PISA administrations between 2012 and 2022 for the selected industrialized countries (Canada, United States, Australia, New Zealand, and a set of European countries). For comparability across years, the authors restrict outcomes to three non-cognitive constructs: sense of belonging (BELONG) measured from 2012 onward; growth mindset and being frequently bullied measured from 2018 onward (so the time trend is excluded for those two outcomes). The regression specifications compare the 2022 cohort to earlier cohorts using a COVID-19 indicator (COVIDt=1 for 2022, 0 for previous years), and they include country fixed effects and country-specific time trends where feasible. Standard errors are clustered at the school level, and inference follows OECD-recommended Balance Repeated Replication (RBB) procedures.

main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression (Table 1 / Table A5). COVID-19 coefficient: +0.049* (Table 1, spec. 1) and −0.040*** (Table A5, spec. 1 with reference years 2018–2022). R-squared: 0.029 (Table 1) and 0.037 (Table A5 spec. 1). Standard errors clustered at the school level.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012–2022 pooled data for the sense of belonging (BELONG) index, the study leveraged COVID-19 period indicator, socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, migrant status, and teacher shortage to model changes in students’ sense of belonging, finding that the pandemic effect differs by comparison window (positive in the longer 2012–2022 comparison but negative in the 2018–2022 short-term window). This indicates that policy responses should distinguish short-run emotional/relational disruptions from longer-run recovery dynamics when designing post-closure student well-being supports.

main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression (Table 1 / Table A5). COVID-19 coefficient: −0.080*** (Table 1, spec. 2) and −0.107*** (Table A5, spec. 4 with reference years 2018–2022). R-squared: 0.028 (Table 1) and 0.027 (Table A5 spec. 4). Standard errors clustered at the school level.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018–2022 pooled data for the growth mindset outcome, the study leveraged COVID-19 period indicator, socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, migrant status, and teacher shortage to estimate pandemic-related changes, finding a statistically significant decline in growth mindset (i.e., shift toward a more fixed mindset) associated with COVID-19. This indicates that education systems should prioritize growth-mindset oriented instructional and counseling practices during and after disruptions, especially for groups showing larger mindset shifts.

main_findings.target_variable: Being frequently bullied (binary, last decile of bullying index)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression (Table 1 / Table A5). COVID-19 coefficient: −0.050*** (Table 1, spec. 3) and −0.043*** (Table A5, spec. 5 with reference years 2018–2022). R-squared: 0.013 (Table 1) and 0.012 (Table A5 spec. 5). Standard errors clustered at the school level.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018–2022 pooled data for the binary frequently-bullied outcome, the study leveraged COVID-19 period indicator, socioeconomic status (ESCS), gender, migrant status, and weeks fully closed to estimate pandemic-related changes, finding that COVID-19 is associated with a significant reduction in the probability of being frequently bullied. This indicates that while physical bullying may have decreased during closures, schools should still address relational and online bullying risks as part of comprehensive post-pandemic student safety strategies.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA non-cognitive outcomes across 2012–2022 (sense of belonging) and 2018–2022 (growth mindset and frequently bullied) for Canada, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, and a set of European countries. Using weighted OLS regressions with country fixed effects, time trends, and OECD-recommended Balance Repeated Replication (RBB) procedures (standard errors clustered at the school level), the authors compare the 2022 cohort to earlier cohorts via a COVID-19 indicator. They find a short-term decline in sense of belonging (e.g., −0.040 SD for 2018–2022) but evidence of recovery in longer comparisons, a significant decline in growth mindset (COVID coefficient around −0.080 SD), and a significant reduction in the likelihood of being frequently bullied (about −0.050 in the 2018–2022 comparison). The paper does not report a missing-data strategy, and the analysis is not ML-based (no predictive algorithms or PV handling), limiting interpretability for causal claims about mechanisms.
